title: The board
goal: A stroke is a chord: several keys down at once, then released together.

head: Zone
Keys
Job
rows: `S T K P W H R`
`F R P B L G T S D Z`
`+` is the top half of the `S` key, above `S-`. Struck with a stroke to continue a word. `*` is the tiebreaker (lesson 9).

blocks.x: The left `S` key is split in two: `+` on top, `S-` below. The `*` is one tall key. The bar across the top is the `#` number bar, which lyk strokes do not use. Keys are grey until they are part of a stroke: colour only ever means *held*. The rest are top and bottom pairs. Each finger owns a column: the top key is `T P H` / `F P L T D`, the bottom `K W R` / `R B G S Z`.
Strike or click keys. The label shows the stroke in steno order, and what the dictionary calls it if it is a word.
However you press them, keys are always written left to right in the same order:

rows: `S T K P W H R`
`F R P B L G T S D Z`

blocks.x: That is why [[PHAP]] is *map* and not *pam*. The same letter can sit on both sides (`R`, `P`, `T`, `S`), so a stroke with no vowel and only right-hand keys is written with a hyphen: [[-T]] is T on the right, [[T]] is T on the left.
Hands only move one way: left hand starts the sound, right hand ends it. If a word's sounds come in that order, it fits in one stroke.

items: Press all the keys of a stroke at roughly the same time. Order does not matter.
The stroke is sent when **every** key is up again.
Hold `Q` (the `+` key, above `S-`) with a stroke for the join key. [[+-G]] is `Q` and `L` together: `L` is the right-hand `-G` key.

blocks.q: How is T on the right hand written alone?
blocks.why: The hyphen says: right-hand keys only.

drill.title: Read the stroke, strike it
drill.x: Each prompt is a stroke written the way steno writes it: left hand, then thumbs, then right hand, a dash where it is needed. Strike those keys together, then let go, and see the word you made. The keys light up after a miss. 90% first try passes.
